## Why This Question Matters

If you are a student picking which languages or tools to learn next, or a bootcamp
grad deciding where to focus your last few weeks of prep, the honest answer to
"what should I learn?" usually comes from someone's personal impression of the job
market rather than from data. Job boards like LinkedIn or Indeed are largely closed
to scraping and heavily curated by algorithms that decide what you see.

Hacker News runs a different kind of job board: once a month, an automated post
titled **"Ask HN: Who is hiring?"** invites companies to post an open role directly
as a comment, with no algorithm ranking, hiding, or paywalling the results. Every
comment is public, plain-text, and follows a loose community convention (location,
remote/on-site, and enough detail about the role that a technical reader can decide
whether to apply). That makes it an unusually clean, real-world source for asking:
**which technical skills come up most often in real job postings this month, and what
does that suggest about where to spend your learning time?**

## Data Source and Ethical Considerations

Hacker News is a public forum with no login wall on its content, and its `robots.txt`
does not block crawling of comment pages. The threads themselves explicitly invite
public commentary and analysis of hiring trends -- there is a long history of
community-built tools that summarize these exact threads (the lecture demo we saw for
Wikipedia GDP tables uses the same `rvest` mental model). To stay within good
scraping practice:

- I make **one request** for the thread's comment page and save a raw HTML snapshot,
  rather than re-requesting the page every time I re-run the analysis.
- I only collect **already-public text** that companies voluntarily posted to be seen;
  no personal profile data, emails, or private information is scraped beyond what a
  company chose to put directly in its own job ad.
- I record the source URL and the date I accessed it, per the reproducibility
  practices from class.

## Step 1: Find the Current Thread Automatically

Rather than hard-coding a specific month's URL (which would make this analysis stale
the moment I publish it), I use Hacker News's public Algolia search API -- itself an
official, documented endpoint, not scraping -- just to look up the **ID** of the most
recent "Who is hiring?" post. The actual data collection in Step 2 is done entirely
with `rvest` against the HTML comment page, which is what this assignment asks for.

```{r find-thread}
RAW_DIR <- here("data", "raw")
RESULTS_DIR <- here("results")
dir.create(RAW_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(RESULTS_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

search_result <- request("http://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search_by_date") |>
  req_url_query(tags = "story,author_whoishiring") |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

thread_id  <- search_result$hits[[1]]$objectID
thread_title <- search_result$hits[[1]]$title
thread_url <- paste0("https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=", thread_id)

thread_title
thread_url
```

## Step 2: Read the Thread with rvest and Save a Raw Snapshot

```{r scrape-and-save}
raw_html_file <- here("data", "raw", paste0("hn_hiring_", thread_id, ".html"))

page <- read_html(thread_url)
write_html(page, raw_html_file)
```

Saving the raw HTML means that if HN's page layout changes next semester, or if I
want to re-check my parsing later, I can re-parse this exact snapshot without making
another request to the site.

## Step 3: Extract Only Top-Level Job Postings

Hacker News nests replies under each comment. A reply asking "is this remote?" is
not a job posting, so I need to keep only **top-level** comments -- the ones written
directly by a hiring company. HN marks each comment's nesting depth with an
`indent` attribute on a small table cell, so I can filter on that rather than
guessing from comment length.

```{r extract-comments}
comment_rows <- page |> html_elements("tr.athing.comtr")

indent_level <- comment_rows |>
  html_element("td.ind") |>
  html_attr("indent") |>
  as.numeric()

comment_text <- comment_rows |>
  html_element("span.commtext") |>
  html_text2()

comment_id <- comment_rows |> html_attr("id")

jobs_raw <- tibble(
  comment_id = comment_id,
  indent     = indent_level,
  text       = comment_text
) |>
  filter(indent == 0, !is.na(text), str_length(text) > 100)

nrow(jobs_raw)
```

Filtering to `indent == 0` keeps only the original postings; the `str_length` check
drops a handful of near-empty or deleted comments that occasionally remain in the
thread.

## Step 4: Clean the Text and Count Skill Mentions

Job ads are free text, so "which skills are requested" has to be defined
operationally: I build a list of common technical skill keywords and, for each
posting, check whether each keyword appears (case-insensitive, matched as a whole
word so "R" doesn't match inside "Restaurant").

```{r keyword-counts}
skills <- c(
  "Python", "JavaScript", "TypeScript", "Java", "Go", "Rust", "C\\+\\+",
  "SQL", "React", "Node", "AWS", "GCP", "Azure", "Docker", "Kubernetes",
  "Ruby", "Rails", "Django", "PostgreSQL", "MongoDB", "Machine Learning",
  "PyTorch", "TensorFlow", "LLM", "Swift", "Kotlin"
)

skill_counts <- map_dfr(skills, function(skill) {
  pattern <- regex(paste0("\\b", skill, "\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE)
  tibble(
    skill = str_remove(skill, "\\\\"),
    n_postings = sum(str_detect(jobs_raw$text, pattern))
  )
}) |>
  arrange(desc(n_postings)) |>
  mutate(share_of_postings = n_postings / nrow(jobs_raw))

skill_counts
```

## Step 5: Visualize the Results

```{r skill-chart, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
skill_counts |>
  slice_max(n_postings, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(skill, n_postings), y = n_postings)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c3e50") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most-Requested Technical Skills in the Current\nHN 'Who Is Hiring' Thread",
    subtitle = paste0("Based on ", nrow(jobs_raw), " job postings, scraped ", Sys.Date()),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of job postings mentioning this skill"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

*(Run this after Knitting to see the actual current-month numbers -- the whole point
of pulling the thread ID programmatically is that this chart updates itself every
time you rerun the analysis.)*

## Step 6: Save the Cleaned Data and Provenance

```{r save-output}
skill_counts |>
  mutate(
    source        = thread_title,
    source_url    = thread_url,
    n_postings_total = nrow(jobs_raw),
    accessed_at   = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z")
  ) |>
  write.csv(here("results", "skill_counts.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## Interpreting the Results

A few things are worth noting about what this kind of count can and cannot tell you.
First, HN's hiring thread skews toward startups and technically-minded companies, so
it is not a representative sample of the entire U.S. labor market the way BLS data
would be -- it is a snapshot of one particular, fairly technical hiring channel.
Second, a skill being *mentioned* is not the same as it being *required*; some ads
list a long stack of "nice to haves." Even with those caveats, the relative ranking
across skills within this one channel, month over month, is a reasonable signal of
which tools are currently table stakes for a software or data role versus which are
more niche.

## Takeaway

If you are deciding what to spend your next few weeks of self-study on, the
languages and frameworks that show up in the largest share of postings in a thread
like this are a defensible, if imperfect, place to start -- and because this analysis
pulls the current month's thread automatically rather than a fixed snapshot, rerunning
it a year from now will tell you whether that ranking has actually shifted, rather
than repeating today's answer forever.
